explain.say: A compost heap is a rotting machine powered by living things. Kitchen scraps and garden waste go in at the top, and dark, crumbly compost comes out at the bottom.

faq.q: What lives in a compost heap?
faq.a: Billions of bacteria and fungi, plus bigger helpers like worms, woodlice, millipedes, springtails and mites. Together they eat and break down the scraps.

faq.q: Why does a compost heap get hot?
faq.a: Bacteria give off heat as they feed and multiply, just as our bodies are warm. In a big heap the heat is trapped, so the centre can reach 55 to 70 degrees Celsius.
A well-mixed hot heap that is turned regularly can be ready in a few months; a cool heap left alone can take a year or more.
A mix of greens, like fruit and vegetable scraps and grass cuttings, and browns, like dry leaves, cardboard and straw. Greens supply nitrogen, browns supply carbon, and the microbes need both.

faq.q: Why do you turn a compost heap?
faq.a: Turning mixes in fresh air. The fast-working bacteria need oxygen; without it, slower microbes take over and the heap can start to smell bad.

facts: Hot compost heaps can reach 55 to 70 degrees Celsius in the middle.
Compost needs a mix of nitrogen-rich greens and carbon-rich browns, plus air and moisture.
The heat in a compost heap comes from microbes respiring as they break down the waste.
